unsupported_self_claims.quote: For the past three years I've worked on transit ridership data
unsupported_self_claims.why: This summarizes roughly 14 months as an analyst plus a 12-month part-time RA, with a gap and a non-transit internship in between, as three continuous years. It is the single-total inflation that F12 warns against, though the parts are listed later in the letter.

M1.notes: Most facts stay within boundaries: workshop paper, first author, correct MAPE numbers, internship model handed off and explicitly not deployed, M.S. expected Dec 2026. The only issue is the 'past three years' framing, which leans toward the inflated total the JD's 2+ years requirement invites.

M2.lead_interest: The gap between what people believe a data system does with their data and what it actually does, centered on people's mental models of how their consented data is aggregated, combined, and modeled downstream.
M2.notes: The Khoury section is an unfilled placeholder, so there are no claims about Prof. Li to evaluate, and the motivation story and facts stay within their boundaries. Some minor unverified specifics (the '2023 holdout', the reviewer-prompted lag re-run, and 'three years learning how these systems are built') are not in the ground truth but do not match any listed violation.

REV.lead_interest: Understanding what people believe data systems are doing with their data and on their behalf (e.g., what someone who tapped 'allow' once pictures about later use), what happens when those beliefs are wrong, and whether disclosures or consent designs could meaningfully change that picture.
REV.notes: The material stays within fact boundaries: the RA observation is framed as informal and blameless, the HCDS work is labeled a small class project, and the M.S. is still in progress. The Khoury faculty section is an unfilled placeholder, so there are no faculty claims; the lead interest is broadened to beliefs about data use and consent but stays close to the ground-truth inference/visibility question.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: I've also done a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool
unsupported_self_claims.why: Calls the AutoML work a study without saying it was a class project (team of 3, 5 classmates, unpublished).

M3.lead_interest: The gap between what people believe data systems do with their data, including what can be inferred about them, and what those systems actually do.

cross_material_inconsistencies: AutoML participant finding: REV says "Two participants assumed the tool already knew which columns in their data were sensitive," while M3 says "some participants assumed the tool protected sensitive data when it didn't." Knowing which columns are sensitive is not the same claim as protecting sensitive data.

Authorship of the usability study: REV says "my team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates" and calls it "a small class project," while M3 says "I've also done a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool" without mentioning the team or the class context. This is a minor shift toward sole credit.
cross.revision_change_summary: REV drops the résumé-style material (metrics, job titles, first-author paper, numbered research agenda) and recasts the applicant as someone driven by a lingering human question ("what did they think they were agreeing to?"), openly saying they have no full research agenda yet.
regressions: M2's framing that users "trusted protections the tool didn't offer" (research question 2, "Assumed safeguards") was softened in REV to participants assuming the tool "knew which columns in their data were sensitive." It returns in M3 as "assumed the tool protected sensitive data when it didn't."

M2's detail that the vendor data "came from partner apps with opt-in consent" was reduced in REV to "apps on people's phones" with "a one-time opt-in." It returns in M3 as "the data came from partner apps with a one-time opt-in."
